zh: 看一段从某个基准高度 b 往上要涂的连续板，宽 w、最低高度 m。只有两种合理做法：每块板都竖涂一次，共 w 笔；或者先用 m−b 笔横涂这段共同的底层，再把高于 m 的部分拆成若干独立的连续子段分别处理。高度为 0 的板天然把围栏切开。
这给出递推：费用 = min(w, m−b + 各子段费用之和)。直接按最小值递归在最坏情况下是平方级，可以改用高度严格递增的单调栈，栈中每个节点记录高度、宽度和已经结算完的子段费用，等高节点合并。

栈底放高度 0 的哨兵。读入新高度 h 时，弹出所有高于 h 的节点：父层基准是 max(h, 弹出后的栈顶高度)，按 min(width, cost+height−base) 结算，再把宽度和费用并入父节点（若父层就是 h，则先暂存到将要插入的新节点）。与栈顶等高就直接合并。最后再追加一个宽度 0、高度 0 的虚拟边界关闭剩余节点，哨兵的累计费用就是答案。height−base+cost 要用 64 位计算，节点尽量紧凑以免超内存。
en: Look at a run of consecutive boards that still needs paint above some base height b, with width w and minimum height m. There are only two sensible plans: paint every board vertically, w strokes in total; or first spend m−b horizontal strokes on the shared bottom layer, then split the part above m into independent consecutive sub-runs and handle each one separately. Boards of height 0 naturally cut the fence apart.

That gives the recurrence cost = min(w, m−b + sum of the sub-run costs). Recursing on the minimum directly is quadratic in the worst case; instead use a monotonic stack with strictly increasing heights, where each node stores its height, width and the cost of the sub-runs already closed, and nodes of equal height are merged.

Put a height-0 sentinel at the bottom of the stack. When a new height h arrives, pop every node taller than h: the parent base is max(h, height of the new stack top), settle the node with min(width, cost+height−base), and add its width and cost to the parent (if the parent level is h itself, hold them in the node about to be pushed). If the top has height h, just merge. At the end append a virtual boundary of width 0 and height 0 to close everything; the sentinel's accumulated cost is the answer. Compute height−base+cost in 64 bits and keep nodes compact to stay within memory.

explanationEn:
## Original source and full input range

The pinned fastprep/Gemini/gemini-minimum-fence-painting-operations.md defines adjacent vertical boards of width 1. A vertical stroke paints one entire board from bottom to top in one go; a horizontal stroke paints a one-unit-high area across several consecutive boards at the same height in one go, and horizontal strokes may only cover areas that are not yet painted. A vertical stroke still paints the whole board, and the original does not forbid it from covering parts already painted horizontally; the restriction on horizontal strokes must not be wrongly extended to vertical strokes. This problem has no source examples; the three public examples are all constructed by this site and do not pretend to be original outputs.

The original source states n≥1 and that heights are non-negative integers, with no numeric upper bound. Based on the original int[] parameter, this site explicitly uses non-negative signed 32-bit heights 0..2147483647; this is a type adaptation, not a decimal constraint from the original. n has no extra small cap: every valid input within the existing 32MiB standard-input budget is accepted; there is no empty-array extension. Standard input is n followed by exactly n heights separated by whitespace; it may end with EOF right after the last number, or with LF/CRLF. In the shortest decimal encoding, n=16777212 one-digit heights with no trailing newline take exactly 33554432 bytes, and the tests cover this boundary; this is derived from the transfer budget, not an upper bound on n from the original problem.

Public examples: [1,2,1] takes two strokes: paint the bottom layer of all three boards horizontally, then paint the middle board vertically (which is allowed to cover its bottom layer); [0,0,0] needs no operation; [2147483647,2147483647] needs only 2 strokes by painting both boards vertically.

## Interval recurrence and streaming implementation

For a run of boards above the current base height b, let its width be w and its minimum height m. You can paint everything vertically with w strokes; or first spend m−b horizontal strokes on the shared bottom layer, then handle the consecutive sub-runs higher than m. So the cost is min(w, m−b+sum of the sub-run costs). Zero-height boards naturally separate the positive-height runs.

Use a monotonic stack with strictly increasing heights to represent intervals that are not yet closed, merging nodes of equal height. A node stores only height, width, and the cost of sub-runs already closed. When a new height h arrives, pop the nodes taller than h; the parent base is max(h, height of the stack top after popping); settle the node with the recurrence above and add it to the parent. If the parent level is exactly the new h, the cost is held in the node about to be inserted; otherwise it is merged into the existing stack top. Equal heights directly merge width and sub-run cost. Finally, a virtual boundary of width 0 and height 0 closes the remaining nodes without adding any board. The accumulated cost of the height-0 sentinel is the answer.

## Proof of correctness

First prove the recurrence is a lower bound. If every board of an interval received a vertical stroke, there are at least w operations. Otherwise some board received no vertical stroke, and every unit of height of that board from b to m must be painted by a horizontal stroke, so there are at least m−b horizontal strokes on these bottom layers. The different consecutive sub-runs above m are separated by boards of height m; no horizontal stroke above that height can cross those boards, and a vertical stroke belongs to only one board. Therefore, after the horizontal strokes needed for the shared bottom layer, each sub-run still needs at least its own optimal cost. Vertical strokes on the lowest boards or extra bottom-layer horizontal strokes can only increase the cost and do not break the lower bound.

Both upper bounds are achievable: painting everything vertically uses w operations; or first paint horizontally the m−b unpainted bottom layers of the whole interval, then use the optimal plan of each sub-run separately. The later horizontal strokes all fall on unpainted areas, and later vertical strokes may paint whole boards under the original rules. So the smaller of the two is the optimal cost.

Popping the stack top means its consecutive interval has met a boundary on the right that is not taller; the lower stack node on the left and the current h together determine the parent base. The costs of the taller sub-runs already popped have been accumulated into this node, so settling it is exactly the recurrence above. Merging equal heights only merges intervals that share a base, keeping total width and sub-run cost, and does not change the recurrence. By induction on the popping order, every settlement is correct; the final zero boundary settles every positive-height interval, so the sentinel's cost is the optimum for the whole fence.

## Complexity, integers and memory

Each board is pushed and popped at most once: time O(n), stack space O(n), with streaming input, no height array and no recursion. The answer is at most n (at most one vertical stroke per board), and node width and cost never exceed n; height is a non-negative int32. When computing height−base+cost, first widen to uint64 to avoid intermediate overflow when heights are close to INT_MAX.

A reference node is exactly 12 bytes, and a single reserve(n+1) avoids keeping both the old and new arrays during growth. Even at the largest transferable n, the required node capacity is only 201326556 bytes, below 256MiB; the program holds neither the input string nor a second n-element array. The strictly increasing deep stack is additionally tested with multi-digit heights close to the budget. The package's limits are 5 seconds and 256MiB; actual Linux sandbox evidence comes from an independent acceptance process, and local records do not pretend to be server results.

## Independent verification

For small domains, BFS runs directly on a painted bitmap of every unit cell: a vertical stroke sets all cells of a board (repainting allowed), and horizontal strokes enumerate every valid consecutive, still-unpainted segment within one row; it finds the shortest path to the fully painted state. Another oracle enumerates the interval-minimum recurrence directly without using the reference's monotonic stack. The independent BFS exhausts n=1..5 with heights 0..2, the interval oracle further exhausts n=1..5 with heights 0..3, and the reference is actually run on them. 163 unique small-oracle cases use BFS or interval enumeration, including random data from fixed seeds. Full-input boundaries use closed forms: all 1s gives 1, a strictly increasing positive sequence gives n, and alternating zeros and tall boards gives the number of positive boards; large plateaus and deep descents are also checked independently. The three negative controls respectively ignore vertical strokes, subtract the base incorrectly, and paint every board vertically on its own; each must exit normally on all formal tests to count as killed. The first negative control computes the purely horizontal cost as the 64-bit sum of positive height differences rather than with a slow stroke-by-stroke simulation.
